Bitcoin hardware wallet maker Coinkite has released its postmortem on Coldcard’s seed-generation flaw, confirming that attackers reconstructed private keys offline rather than compromising the devices. A firmware configuration error disabled the hardware random number generator, causing devices to rely on an insecure pseudorandom number generator. At least 15 independent review and security research efforts between 2021 and 2026 failed to identify the flaw, including a review using OpenAI’s Cybersecurity Harness.

Coinkite received 300 loss-related support tickets involving 236 customer accounts, approximately 0.2% of its estimated user base. According to Galaxy Research, 1,778.84 BTC were stolen from over 8,600 addresses, worth approximately $107 million at current prices. Coinkite released patched firmware on July 31 but warned that firmware updates cannot secure previously affected seeds. The attackers remain unidentified, and Coinkite has yet to decide whether to compensate affected customers. — link

Bitcoin hardware wallet maker Coinkite has released its postmortem on Coldcard’s seed-generation flaw, confirming that attackers reconstructed private keys offline rather than compromising the devices. A firmware configuration error disabled the hardware random number generator, causing devices to rely on an insecure pseudorandom number generator. At least 15 independent review and security research efforts between 2021 and 2026 failed to identify the flaw, including a review using OpenAI’s Cybersecurity Harness.

Coinkite received 300 loss-related support tickets involving 236 customer accounts, approximately 0.2% of its estimated user base. According to Galaxy Research, 1,778.84 BTC were stolen from over 8,600 addresses, worth approximately $107 million at current prices. Coinkite released patched firmware on July 31 but warned that firmware updates cannot secure previously affected seeds. The attackers remain unidentified, and Coinkite has yet to decide whether to compensate affected customers. — link

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced on November 23 a proposed 22nd sanctions package against Russia, seeking to extend transaction bans to approximately 60 Russian banks and remove them from the SWIFT system. The proposal also targets cryptocurrency platforms and payment networks in Russia and third countries facilitating sanctions evasion. Von der Leyen said the EU has launched a Crypto Sanctions Task Force to strengthen enforcement. Additional measures include expanded energy restrictions, sanctions targeting Russia's shadow fleet, and a ban on EU citizens holding management positions in Russian companies. The package remains subject to approval. — link
